title: Knowledge Check 7: Lessons 49-56
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 49-56 of the salesforce-architect series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: A team transfers a set of components to another org as an unmanaged package. What does the receiving org end up with?
options: A one-time copy it owns, with no versioning and no upgrade path
A source-protected bundle the originator hides from every receiver
A locked bundle only the originator can later modify or upgrade
A versioned bundle the originator can upgrade on demand
questions.explanation: An unmanaged package is a one-time copy: after install its components belong to the receiving org, editable and deletable, with no link back to the source and no way to push an upgrade. Locked components, source protection, and upgrade paths belong to managed packages.

questions.question: Which package type is versioned and upgradeable yet keeps its components editable in the target org with an optional namespace?
options: Managed package
Unmanaged package
Unlocked package
First-generation package
questions.explanation: Unlocked packages are built for a team's own estate: versioned and upgradeable like managed packages, but their metadata stays editable in the target org and a namespace is optional. Managed packages lock components and require a namespace, and unmanaged packages offer no versioning.

questions.question: The platform ships three major releases a year that land automatically in every org. What does this ask of an architect planning a package release?
options: Opting the whole org out of releases that conflict with a deployment plan
Testing packaged components in the preview sandbox before rollout
Buying extra platform capacity to absorb each automatic release
Registering the package on the AppExchange before every release
questions.explanation: Because releases arrive automatically on a fixed calendar and cannot be declined, the architect confirms the org's maintenance window does not conflict and rehearses packaged components in the sandbox preview window before production receives the release.

questions.question: Pre-launch testing is not sufficient as a governance control for an AI system. Why?
options: Model behavior stays fixed after ship, so a single sign-off is enough
Its behavior drifts as data or the vendor's version changes over time
Reviewing lower-risk systems is prohibited by regulation
Model outputs stay correct in production however they were tested
questions.explanation: A model is not stable after ship: its output distribution shifts as the data or the vendor's version changes, so governance needs ongoing monitoring as part of the structure, not only a pre-launch check.

questions.question: Which set names the four functions of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework?
options: Design, Build, Test, Deploy
Plan, Do, Check, Act
Govern, Map, Measure, Manage
Collect, Store, Model, Monitor
questions.explanation: The framework organizes AI risk work into Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage, run as a continuous loop rather than a single pass. Govern establishes accountability and policy, Map names context and failure modes, Measure evaluates risk, and Manage acts and feeds findings back.

questions.question: A complete evidence set for reconstructing an AI incident must align which records on the same event?
options: The system-action log, the AI interaction record, and the approval record
The vendor contract, the subscription invoice, and the product marketing brief
Only the final text sent to the customer, with no surrounding context
The encryption key status and the storage tier of the data
questions.explanation: A complete evidence set needs all three: the platform log of system actions, the AI record of the model's reasoning and retrieved context, and the human's approval, aligned on the same event so a past failure can be reconstructed.

questions.question: A team needs basic offline record viewing and simple data entry for internal users, with no custom development. Which approach fits?
options: The Mobile SDK, because any offline capability demands custom development
The standard app with Briefcase, configured declaratively by an admin
A fully disconnected app that never syncs with the server
Cloud-only storage that keeps no data on the device at all
questions.explanation: For internal users following standard record workflows, the standard app with Briefcase covers offline viewing and simple entry declaratively, with no development. The Mobile SDK path is reserved for complex offline workflows, hardware integration, or a custom consumer experience.

questions.question: A device syncs a local edit up while the server holds a newer change to the same record. Which pairing keeps the server authoritative without clobbering either change?
options: Overwrite for sync down and leave-if-changed for sync up
Overwrite for sync up and leave-if-changed for sync down
Overwrite for both sync down and sync up
Leave-if-changed for both sync down and sync up
questions.explanation: Using overwrite for sync down lets server data replace the local copy, while leave-if-changed for sync up preserves a local edit rather than clobbering a newer server change. That pairing keeps the server the single source of truth.

questions.question: A device holding offline customer data is lost. Which set of controls limits the damage?
options: A larger local cache so the data survives the loss
Storing a plaintext password so the user can log back in without delay
Encryption at rest, a device passcode, and a remote wipe
Relying on the phone's default settings to protect the app data
questions.explanation: Encryption at rest keeps the data unreadable without the key, a device passcode keeps that key from being trivially accessible, and device management lets the company remotely wipe the app's data when a device is lost.

questions.question: When can the Salesforce event bus be relied on to deliver events in the order they were published?
options: Across every publish call, regardless of how or when the events were sent
Within a single publish call, but not across separate publish calls
Never, so order can never be reconstructed at all
Only for record-change events, never for platform events
questions.explanation: Order is guaranteed within one publish call, where the batch is delivered in the order it was passed in, but separate publish requests can be handled by different servers and arrive out of order. When order matters downstream, carry it in the payload rather than trust the channel.

questions.question: A subscriber disconnects and later reconnects. How should it recover the events it missed within the retention window?
options: Add one to its last Replay ID and pass that computed value back in
Start fresh and ignore the gap, because the bus drops every event a subscriber missed
Pass back its stored last Replay ID so the bus redelivers from there
Bump a commit number for every reconnect to find the gap
questions.explanation: Replay works by persisting the last successfully processed Replay ID and resubscribing from that stored position, so the bus redelivers everything published after it within the retention window. Replay IDs are opaque and non-contiguous, so they are never computed by arithmetic.

questions.question: The bus delivers at least once, so the same event can arrive twice. Which consumer design keeps a duplicate from double-applying the work?
options: A unique-key dedupe on the event's UUID, atomic with the work
Applying every event as new work and trusting the bus to deliver once
Skipping any event whose Replay ID looks familiar
Checking a seen-list, then applying the work in a later separate step
questions.explanation: Because delivery is at-least-once, duplicates are expected. The fix is an idempotent consumer whose dedupe on the event's UUID is atomic with the work, so two concurrent deliveries cannot both pass the check. Events are identified by UUID, not by Replay ID.

questions.question: A fan-out must call several external systems on every page load, and one is slow. What is the sound first response for a read-side aggregation view?
options: Fire all the calls synchronously and accept that the slow system delays the page
Cache the composed result or move the fan-out off the request path
Raise the per-transaction callout limit above one hundred
Let the browser issue the callouts to each external system directly
questions.explanation: The cumulative time for external callouts in one transaction is bounded, and a slow system consumes budget the others need, so a frequently viewed read-side view should cache the composed answer or push the fan-out off the synchronous path rather than pay the full cost per visit.

questions.question: A single REST call must create related records together. What are the subrequest ceiling and the query cap for a plain Composite request?
options: Up to twenty-five subrequests, at most five of them queries
Up to five subrequests, at most one of them a query
Up to one hundred subrequests with no query cap at all
Up to five hundred subrequests, at most five of them queries
questions.explanation: A plain Composite request carries up to twenty-five subrequests and allows at most five query operations, while a Composite Graph raises the ceiling to five hundred. Both let subrequests reference each other's results by id.

questions.question: Four of five sources respond and one times out on a read-side aggregation view. What should the service return?
options: Nothing until every callout completes, so the user never sees a partial view
A response that silently omits the missing block with no indication
The data plus a status naming the missing source, so the page reads as partial
A full retry of the whole fan-out inside the same transaction until all respond
questions.explanation: A read-side aggregation view should return partial results and flag them: the composed data goes back with a status that marks the response incomplete and names the missing source, so the page tells the truth instead of silently omitting a block.

questions.question: What single principle distinguishes federation from replication when the org needs external data?
options: The data is copied into the org and kept aligned by a pipeline
The data stays at the source and the query is pushed to it
The data is cached in the browser after one full download
The data is loaded nightly into a big object for local querying
questions.explanation: Federation leaves the data in place and moves the computation to it: Salesforce sends the query to the source and renders only the matching rows, whereas replication copies the data in and owns keeping the two copies aligned.

questions.question: What does query pushdown do for a federated query?
options: Translates the WHERE, ORDER BY, and LIMIT into the source's query
Downloads the full external table and filters it inside Salesforce
Copies every matching row into Salesforce storage for later reads
Forces the source into a synchronous write-back for the matched rows
questions.explanation: Pushdown translates the filters, ordering, and pagination from a SOQL query and sends them to the external system, so the source runs the query where the data lives and returns only the matching rows over the wire.

questions.question: Which requirement makes federation the wrong choice?
options: Read-only display of a fresh, authoritative balance on a record page
A low-frequency lookup of clean data that must stay in its source region
An AI assistant that must ground on the external data as if native
A high-governance source that regulation forbids copying into Salesforce
questions.explanation: AI and agent features currently operate on native objects and cannot use external objects as a grounding or activation source, so a requirement that a model read external data as native rules federation out. Writes, cross-object joins, and high-volume access are the other disqualifiers.

questions.question: How does retrieval-augmented generation connect a model to enterprise data?
options: It retrains the model on enterprise documents so it permanently knows them
It retrieves relevant data at answer time and grounds the answer
It replaces the model with a keyword search index over the documents
It stores a full copy of the enterprise data inside the model's weights
questions.explanation: RAG leaves the model's weights unchanged and instead retrieves the relevant enterprise passages at question time, building an augmented prompt from the question and those passages so the answer is grounded in current, authoritative data.

questions.question: A vector index is a derived snapshot over source documents. What does a stale index cause?
options: The model refuses to answer because it cannot retrieve any documents at all
The vector index grows larger than the refresh job can keep up with over time
The model answers confidently from outdated context but looks sourced
The retrieval layer falls back to keyword search on the source
questions.explanation: Because the index is derived from source documents, a change to a source makes the corresponding chunks stale until they are re-embedded. A stale index is worse than no retrieval, because the model still sounds sourced while reporting outdated content.

questions.question: Where does access control belong in a retrieval-augmented stack, and why?
options: On the retrieval layer before generation, limiting what a user can fetch
On the generation output, so the model can redact anything sensitive it produced
Only on the source system, since the index already enforces permissions
After the answer is written, when the user decides what to keep
questions.explanation: The retrieval layer is the filter: restricting what a given questioner can retrieve keeps the model from quoting data the user has no right to see. Access control belongs there, before generation, not on the output or the source alone.

questions.question: Two users read an interface in the same language but have different locales. What differs on their screens?
options: Only the words on the buttons, because the interface language governs everything
The date, time, and number formatting, even though the language is the same
Nothing, because locale and language always change together
Every amount's currency, which is rebuilt for each user's region
questions.explanation: Language controls the words on the interface, while locale controls how values are shaped: dates, times, numbers, names, and addresses. With the same language, users with different locales still see different value formats.

questions.question: With advanced currency management enabled, which conversion does NOT use the dated exchange rate?
options: An opportunity that closed in a month whose rate is on record
An opportunity product line item amount
A currency formula field result on the opportunity
A report on opportunities that shows the converted amount
questions.explanation: Dated exchange rates apply to opportunities and their related objects and reports, but not to currency formula fields, forecasting, currency fields on other objects, or cross-object formulas, which fall back to static conversion.

questions.question: An account's default currency is changed from one currency to another. What happens to its existing amounts?
options: They are not converted, just shown with the new currency code
They are immediately revalued at the current exchange rate
They are converted to the corporate currency and back again
The change is blocked until advanced currency management is on
questions.explanation: Changing a record's default currency does not revalue its amounts; it only changes the currency code they display with. Revaluation is a separate, deliberate operation, not a side effect of the label change.
